124.t: Publisher songs, new arrangers, and more time for Ella
124.s: Shapiro-Bernstein and Mills also supplied songs; McRae hired Jimmy Mundy and Van Alexander and gave Ella more broadcast time.
124.ch: With Chick Webb and Ella Fitzgerald, 1936-39
124.q: And we began to give Ella Fitzgerald most of the broadcast time. Like, she would just sing one song, we would have her doing three -- sometimes four.

124.t: Ella borrowed for Benny Goodman's Camel show
124.s: Goodman wanted Ella for the Robbins hit "Please Be Kind" on his radio show, naming the singers who preceded Helen Forrest.
124.ch: With Chick Webb and Ella Fitzgerald, 1936-39
124.q: popular. It was a number one hit, so he turned around and said, "Hey, I'll get Ella." Asked Chick -- say, "Let me have Ella."

124.t: "A-Tisket, A-Tasket" makes Ella a feature attraction
124.s: Ella was built into a featured act, and "A-Tisket, A-Tasket" gave her a hit.
124.ch: With Chick Webb and Ella Fitzgerald, 1936-39
124.q: double attraction. That was the beginning of (inaudible) her -- when we put all that music behind her, all those big pop songs, all those big hits.

124.t: "Goodnight My Love" and Ella on Goodman's Camel show
124.s: Jack Robbins gave the band the hit first; Ella sight-read arrangements quickly, and Goodman borrowed her and the arrangement for his broadcast.
124.ch: Leading the band after Chick Webb, 1939-40
124.q: Well, this one particular song we had -- the name of the song was "Goodnight My Love." That was the song (inaudible). You asked me on the interview what was the song that Ella did.

124.t: Ella's songs and Robbins's Hollywood tunes
124.s: Ella made every song her own; the band stayed ahead by getting top Hollywood songs, and Chick saw her talent early.
124.ch: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
124.q: you, because when she put her stamp on it, that's it! You know, back in those days when Ella got a song, Ella was the top of all those girls -- all the white girls there.

124.t: Songs selected for Ella from Rust's discography
124.s: Welburn reads titles like "Spring Fever Blues" and McRae confirms they were chosen for her.
124.ch: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
124.q: Remember that? That was a big thing we had that kind of blues type of arrangement to it, you know. It would've broke the tempo down on the end, you know, like a Louie Armstrong (inaudible). That was a big record.

124.t: "Mr. Paganini" and novelty numbers for Ella
124.s: A novelty by a husband-and-wife team shows how Ella could handle any style, with songs sprung on her only when ready.
124.ch: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
124.q: It was kind of a corny thing. See, we picked -- See, Ella could do all types of things. So we would pick -- We would okay different (inaudible) things the fellow like that Mr. Paganini. I remember (inaudible) and her husband wrote that together. And they come up to the Savoy and when -- they were…

124.t: "A-Tisket, A-Tasket" as Ella's own idea; hiring Van Alexander
124.s: The song was Ella's nursery-rhyme number; Van Alexander, hired as pop arranger, wrote it down.
124.ch: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
124.q: : 'A Tisket A Tasket' was Ella's own thing. It was her own idea -- She would That was her thing that (inaudible) sing up in Yonkers or White Plains or wherever she was from. 'A Tisket A Tasket', that's a nursery rhyme. Her and some school kids would do, you know.

379.t: Ella's earliest recordings and A-Tisket, A-Tasket
379.s: They sort out Ella's first records, her Goodman session, and how A-Tisket, A-Tasket made her popular.
379.q: No, no. She record -- she record a song much before that. We went to the -- we went to Boston to the Le Vaggi -- Le Vaggi Restaurant, and I think it was in '36, I think it was. Yeah, in '36, because I just got through -- late '36, '36 or -7. I'm bad on dates. But that -- just like you said, that…

379.t: Ella's success, radio broadcasts and Goodman recording
379.s: Ella becomes a hit, the band broadcasts daily on NBC, and she records with Benny Goodman.
379.q: But, that was the whole idea. So, it the girl MADE gave me such a hit, it was unbelievable. And then this guy started writing for her, just write. He used to play the (inaudible) and arrange it for her to sing. Then she'd sing rag, she'd sing swings all right. So the band start doing like this.…

379.s: He tells how he heard an amateur-contest winner, persuaded Webb to hire her despite her appearance, and she debuted at Yale.
379.q: contest last night in Harlem Opera House, next door. She's a terrific singer, and I would like for you to take Chick up after her. Why don't you bring the girl here, and between the shows we'll go to the (inaudible), you know, in the parlor, the piano and hear her.

0.t: Ella Fitzgerald joins Tiny Bradshaw after the Harlem Opera House contest
0.s: After winning the amateur contest Ella sang with Bradshaw's band, then went back to Chick Webb without a contract.
0.q: We stayed there two years, until they got too big for himself and wanted to try to buck the booking agent -- that was wrong. See, what happened, when Ella Fitzgerald, after she won the amateur contest at the Apollo, we were going -- we had left Chicago, came on through Chicago, through Ohio,…

0.t: Ella Fitzgerald stops the show and Caldwell's advice
0.s: Ella, put on last, took encores; Caldwell encouraged her backstage and warned her about stage-door Johnnies.
0.q: Too big for his britches that time. And, you see, at that gig with us at the Harlem Opera House, she broke up the show. She tied the show up, because we had so many big stars from the Cotton Club was on that show. And they used to put her on last after all the band numbers and all the others --…

382.t: Ella Fitzgerald's reaction to 'Loch Lomond' and the novelty hit
382.s: Maxine says she could not be a second Ella; Ella changed her repertoire after 'Loch Lomond' and needed one hit song.
382.ch: Early recordings and arrival in New York
382.q: Yeah. While I was listening to the vocal, you know, I remembered when I came to New York, Ella Fitzgerald was tops, and she still is as far as I'm concerned. But I think that there was a certain similarity between my style and hers. And, of course, it's nothing to wonder about that because we're…

382.t: Billie Holiday, Ella Logan and the origins of the 'Loch Lomond' idea
382.s: Hughes asks if other singers' folk-song swings inspired it; Maxine discusses Ella Logan and press coverage in DownBeat.
382.ch: Early recordings and arrival in New York
382.q: Actually the time that I did Lock Loehman, I think one of the first efforts -- I'm pretty sure they've been swinging classics forever -- you know, bands (inaudible) as a novelty -- but Tommy Dorsey had just recorded "Song of India," and the interest seemed to have in that direction of swing, you…

961.t: Recording All That Jazz and becoming Ella's accompanist
961.s: He did the sessions after rehearsing with Ella at her house, apparently as a trial set up by Norman Granz, then started touring with her at a lighter schedule.
961.ch: Singers: Sarah Vaughan and Ella Fitzgerald
961.q: No it didn’t. Actually that was the first time I had worked with Ella. I got called to do that session. Actually there were a total of four sessions, I did two of them, Kenny Barron did — I think I did three and Kenny did one or something like that for that CD. And then on the basis — I think as I…

451.t: Academy Awards show and the 1941 Buick
451.s: He played the Oscars with Ella, who missed a note on a key change, and was mistaken for Jack Benny in his Buick.
451.ch: Touring, Ella Fitzgerald and South America
451.q: Academy Awards show… I guess because I was working with Ella and she sang on that show. That’s the only time I ever heard her mess up. There was an arrangement that, big band arrangement. Andre Previn was leading the big band on the Academy Awards. And there was a quick change of key, and I think…

31.t: Harlem Opera House amateur hour, Ella Fitzgerald and Sarah Vaughan
31.s: Retelling how he introduced Ella Fitzgerald to Chick Webb and Sarah Vaughan to Earl Hines, and why he later left amateur hour to an assistant.
31.ch: Reel IV retellings and New York pianists
31.q: Yeah, closer. And we used to have Amateur Hour every Wednesday night and these kids used to come in, you know, and I would find out what they would sing -- I wouldn't rehearse them -- I say to give me a key and start singing, and I'd get the key. So Ella came in there, and so she was going around…

78.t: Singer Viola Jefferson, who outsang Ella with 'A-Tisket A-Tasket'
78.s: Fletcher conducted one Horace Henderson date; singer Viola Jefferson brought the house down at the Chicago Savoy with 'A-Tisket A-Tasket' by selling it with motions.
78.ch: Touring, recording and Fletcher's band in the 1940s
78.q: Yes. She went to Europe, and was quite successful there. She was the girl that outsang Ella Fitzgerald on "Tisket-a-Tasket" with that 5,000 people in the Savoy Ballroom in Chicago.
